title: Raising the sparks
hook: holy sparks hide in everything, and ordinary acts done with care can lift them

segments.voice: Yesterday, niggun, the Hasidic melody with no words. Your line was a song with no words. Did you hum when words ran out? Day three hundred ten.

Most of your day isn't dramatic. You wash a cup. You answer an email. You fold a shirt, buy bread, sweep a floor. It can feel like the real life, the important, spiritual part, is happening somewhere else, and all this is just maintenance. Hasidism took a picture from the kabbalah that turns that upside down. It says hidden inside the cup, the email, the shirt and the bread are sparks of holiness, waiting. And the way you handle them can set them free. Today's word: tikkun.
screen: `WASH A CUP. FOLD A SHIRT.` → `JUST MAINTENANCE?` → `SPARKS HIDDEN IN THE ORDINARY.`

segments.voice: Tikkun means repair, or mending, setting something right. The picture behind it comes from Rabbi Isaac Luria, a kabbalist in the town of Safed, whose teachings were written down mostly by his student, Chaim Vital. In Luria's picture, when God made the world, divine light was poured into vessels that couldn't hold it. The vessels shattered. Sparks of holy light scattered everywhere and fell into the world, trapped in shells, hidden in all things. The work of history is tikkun: gathering those sparks and lifting them back. That sounds cosmic, and it is. But the Baal Shem Tov and the Hasidim brought it down to the kitchen. They taught that sparks wait everywhere: in food, in work, in conversation, even in the people and places you happen to cross. When you eat with a blessing, work honestly, speak kindly, do an ordinary thing with care, you lift the spark inside it. A related phrase is tikkun olam, repairing the world, and it has old roots. The Mishnah uses it for rules made for the good order of society, and the Aleinu prayer speaks of perfecting the world under the kingdom of the Almighty. In modern times it has become a common name for justice and social action. The Hasidic version is quieter. The repair begins with how you wash this cup, right now.
screen: `TIKKUN: REPAIR.` · `LURIA: THE VESSELS SHATTERED.` · `SPARKS IN FOOD, WORK AND WORDS.` · `TIKKUN OLAM: REPAIR THE WORLD.` · then, large: `LIFT THE SPARKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one chore with care. Settle, and breathe. Choose a small task in front of you or coming up soon. Washing a dish. Making a bed. Tidying a desk. When you do it, do it slowly, and fully. Feel the water, the fabric, the weight of things. Imagine there's a spark inside it, waiting for someone to do this well. For now, just picture yourself doing it that way. If you pray, you can say a word of blessing before you begin. The bell holds the time.
Tikkun. Repair. In Luria's picture, holy sparks are scattered through everything, and ordinary acts done with care lift them back.
Your line: lift the sparks. Today, pick one boring task and do it as if something holy were hidden inside it. Day three hundred ten.

howItsDone: Hasidim speak of raising sparks through blessings, prayer and everyday acts done with intention, and in modern usage tikkun olam names acts of justice and repair in the world.

original.note: Hebrew: repair, mending. Tikkun olam: repairing the world.

trapdoor: what you thought: a word for fixing things.
what it means: gathering scattered holy sparks by doing ordinary things with care.

what a scholar hears: Lurianic kabbalah's breaking of the vessels (shevirat ha-kelim) and trapped sparks (nitzotzot), later popularized by Hasidism, with tikkun olam older still in the Mishnah and Aleinu.

sources.ref: Lurianic teaching on the breaking of the vessels and the raising of sparks (as recorded by Chaim Vital)

notes: Lurianic cosmology simplified for a general audience (tzimtzum omitted); a Keeper may want to review the phrasing.
Luria (1534–1572) in Safed; 'fifteen hundreds' used. Chaim Vital as main recorder: confirm.
Mishnah Gittin 4 uses 'mipnei tikkun ha-olam' for rabbinic enactments; confirm the mishnayot cited.
Hasidic teaching on raising sparks through eating and work is attributed broadly to the Baal Shem Tov and his circle; confirm framing.
